opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we think about constantly, honestly. The trap is building a product whose whole value proposition is "we wrapped the current best model in a nice UI." If that's all you are, you're one model release away from irrelevance, because whatever clever workaround you built for a model's limitations six months ago is just baked into the next version.

So the way I frame it is: assume the models get dramatically better, and ask what still matters in that world. And a few things keep coming up.

First, the workflow and the context around the model. A chemist or a protein engineer isn't just asking "generate me a binder." They're juggling assay data, synthesis constraints, IP considerations, what the team tried last quarter and why it failed. The model is one component inside a much larger decision loop. If you own that loop, meaning you're where the data lives and where decisions get made and recorded, then better models make your product *more* valuable, not less. You become the place where the new capability gets plugged in.

Second, the connection to the physical world. Molecular design isn't like writing code where you can verify instantly. Eventually something has to get made and tested in a wet lab, and that feedback is slow, expensive, and noisy. Closing that loop well, so experimental results flow back and actually inform the next round, is a hard problem that doesn't disappear when the generative model improves. If anything, as generation gets cheap, the bottleneck shifts even more to validation and prioritization.

Third, and this is a bit of a discipline thing internally: we try not to over-invest in features that exist purely to compensate for model weaknesses. If we're building elaborate scaffolding because the model can't handle some constraint today, we ask whether that's a six-month problem or a five-year problem. If it's a six-month problem, we build the lightest possible version and expect to throw it away.

And I'd say the flip side is that you have to be genuinely model-agnostic. You can't marry one architecture. The field moves too fast. Today's state of the art structure predictor or generative model will be superseded, so the system has to make swapping that piece in and out pretty painless.

So the short version is: build for the scientist's whole problem, not for the model's current gaps. The models are the engine, but people still need the car.

r001.rationale: The response says to build for scientists’ broader workflow and make model-specific scaffolding disposable, but does not frame the software as a bridge enabling research that leads to its successor.

r002.rationale: It discusses experimental validation and prioritization as bottlenecks, but does not describe a shift from inspecting individual designs to orchestrating hypothesis campaigns as molecular-level verification is solved.

r003.rationale: It places models within a broader decision loop, but does not propose composing structure prediction, binding, and design capabilities to manage the broader scientific research cycle.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question we think about constantly, and honestly it's the thing that shapes almost every product decision we make. The way I frame it is: if your product is just a thin wrapper around a model's current capabilities, you're betting against the model getting better, and that's a bet you'll lose every time.

So the way we think about it is to separate what the model does from what the chemist actually needs to do. A medicinal chemist doesn't wake up in the morning wanting a better binding affinity predictor. They want to get a molecule to the clinic. That involves a whole workflow: proposing ideas, filtering them against synthesizability, ADMET, IP, what the team has already tried, coordinating with the people who actually have to make the compound, and then closing the loop when the assay data comes back. The model is one piece of that, and a lot of the rest is data plumbing, interfaces, and institutional memory that doesn't get obsoleted when the model improves. If anything, better models make that infrastructure more valuable because now you're pulling more throughput through it.

The second thing is we try to design the software so that model improvement is an upgrade, not a rewrite. The interfaces between the model and the rest of the system are deliberately boring. Structures in, scored or generated structures out, with provenance attached. When a better generative model or a better property predictor lands, we swap it in and the chemist's workflow doesn't change. We've already done this a few times internally, and each time the user mostly experiences it as "the suggestions got better," which is exactly what you want.

And then the third piece, which I think is underrated, is the data flywheel. Every time a chemist accepts, rejects, or modifies a suggestion, that's signal. Every assay result that comes back is labeled data in a domain where labeled data is scarce and expensive. A general-purpose model trained on public data can't see any of that. So the moat isn't the model, it's the loop. The better the model gets, the more decisions flow through our system, and the more proprietary signal we capture about what actually works in a specific program.

I'll be honest that there's a category of features that does get obsoleted, and we try to be clear-eyed about that. Anything that's essentially "we hand-engineered a heuristic because the model wasn't good enough yet" is on a clock. We build those when customers need them today, but we try not to over-invest in them and we try to be honest with ourselves about when to rip them out. The failure mode is falling in love with your clever workaround and defending it after the model has made it unnecessary.

So the short version: build the thing that gets more valuable as models improve, not the thing that competes with them. Own the workflow and the feedback loop, keep the model layer swappable, and treat your heuristics as temporary scaffolding rather than the building.

r001.rationale: The response calls hand-engineered heuristics temporary scaffolding and says some features may be replaced, but it does not frame the software as a bridge enabling research that leads to its successor.

r002.rationale: It describes workflows, throughput, and feedback loops, but does not anticipate a shift from inspecting individual designs to orchestrating hypothesis campaigns as molecular verification is solved.

r003.rationale: It mentions generative models, property predictors, and the broader medicinal chemistry workflow, but does not propose composing structure prediction, binding, and design capabilities to manage the scientific research cycle.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to build with the assumption that the models are going to get better. If your entire product is a workaround for something a model can’t do today, that’s a pretty fragile place to be.

For molecular design, I’d start with the scientist’s workflow: What are they trying to achieve? What constraints matter? How do they decide what to make and test next? The model is one component of that process. Better predictions or better generation can be incredibly valuable, but you still need to connect those capabilities to an experiment and then bring the results back into the next decision.

So I’d want the software to make it easy to adopt a better model, and I’d be willing to throw away features when that model makes them unnecessary. The durable thing you’re building is the connection between a scientist’s intent, the computational tools, and the experimental feedback. If model progress makes that whole loop more useful, then it’s helping your product.

r002.rationale: It discusses connecting models to experiments and feedback, but not a shift from inspecting individual designs to orchestrating hypothesis campaigns as molecular verification is solved.

r003.rationale: It mentions predictions, generation, and experimental feedback, but does not propose composing structure prediction, binding, and design capabilities to manage the broader research cycle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to assume the models are going to get better. If your product depends on a particular limitation of today’s models sticking around, that’s a pretty fragile place to be.

So I’d separate the things that a better model should replace from the things it makes more valuable. You might build a feature today to help someone search through candidate molecules, and eventually the model can do that much more directly. That’s fine. The underlying need is still there: a scientist has an objective, a bunch of constraints, and experimental results they need to make sense of before deciding what to try next.

The software should make that loop easier. How do you express what you want? How do you evaluate a suggestion? How do you bring the experimental feedback back into the next round? Better models can make that whole workflow more powerful.

You still have to build something useful today. But I’d rather build something where a new model lets us give the scientist a better experience than something where a new model is a threat to the business.

r001.rationale: The response says today’s features may be replaced and emphasizes building software that benefits from better models, but it does not frame the software as a bridge enabling research that leads to its successor.

r002.rationale: It describes a scientist’s workflow across suggestions and experimental feedback, but does not describe a shift from inspecting individual designs to orchestrating hypothesis campaigns as molecular verification becomes solved.

r003.rationale: It discusses supporting the research loop, but does not propose composing structure prediction, binding, and design capabilities to manage the broader scientific cycle.
